newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Rate clues in U.S. data post - payrolls.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Rate clues in U.S. data post - payrolls.

text.p: Speculation about a U.S. interest rate rise after Friday's robust August payroll report looks set to dominate economic markets in the week ahead, analysts said.
The 250,000 gain in non-farm payrolls and a six cent rise in average hourly earnings knocked Treasuries and European bonds into a brief tailspin on Friday from which they soon recovered.

Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International, said the market focus next week would be on the remaining pieces of economic data which the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will have in front of it when it meets on September 24.
These include July consumer credit figures on Monday, the Beige book on U.S. economic conditions on Wednesday, August consumer and producer prices on Thursday and August retail sales on Friday.

"Even if next week's indicators are weak, it is hard to see the Fed sitting on its hands once again as it would be seen as behind the inflation curve and there would be an adverse reaction on treasury markets," Edmonds said.
Edmonds said the focus in Europe would be on budget preparations in countries including France, Sweden, Spain and the Netherlands.
The main concern here was whether budgets were credible and consistent with the Maastricht Treaty on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Sean Shepley, international economist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said British inflation numbers due out next week were likely to stay muted, but probably would not be as benign as in previous months, especially Monday's producer prices for August.
He said the debate would continue on how strong and how inflationary current growth was in the British economy.

Shepley said that in France, August CPI on Friday should continue a downtrend in its annual rate, especially since the increase in value-added tax in August 1995 would now drop out of the latest 12-month period.
He tipped reasonably swift convergence over the next six months or so in German and French CPI levels.
But he cautioned that this had limited signifigance in ensuring stability for the French franc since France's main worry was to ensure adequate economic growth, rather than concerns about inflation.

Shepley said that no official news was expected out of the European Union's monetary committee meeting starting in Brussels on Monday but markets would pay close attention to preparations for the September 20-21 meeting of EU finance ministers and central bankers in Dublin.
On the back of that meeting, he said some people were looking for an easing of German interest rates and possibly a statement of Franco-German solidarity on EMU.
In Japan, Shepley said markets would continue to focus on rumours about an October election and also the possibility of a supplementary budget.
Mark Capleton, international bond strategist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd, said it was a fairly sparse week for data on continental Europe.
Capleton said there would be some interest in Spain's CPI figure for August which is due from Thursday.

Capleton forecast French August CPI, due out on Friday, would be flat for the month and rise 1.9 percent year-on-year. In Britain, Capleton foresaw a small fall in output price inflation at 1.3 percent year-on-year to August from 1.5 percent year-on-year in July.

Capleton said that such numbers would not in themselves deter the government from seeking an interest rate cut, but this was increasingly unlikely as it would be clearly seen to be opposed by the Bank of England and might have to be reversed before next year's election.
